items.text: One may write upon all things
items.q: This poem is written on a classroom board. Does its first line read as poetry?
before: …is carrying bread, toward Enghelab Square. I reach the entrance to the University of Tehran. I was late. The classroom was full and the latecomers were seated on the floor around the edges. Right by the door I found an empty spot and sat down. On the board, in fine handwriting, they had written:

items.text: write upon the water with your own blood

items.q: In the poem, 'the burned ones' means people consumed by love. Is that clear?
This is the poem's last line. Does it close the poem well?

items.text: You can read it two ways. If we take Hafez to be the summit of ambiguity, I'd say this single mesra is the – the su-summit of ambiguity in Hafez's ow-own words.
items.q: Nervous and excited, Amir stammers as he explains a line of poetry. Does the stammering read naturally?

items.text: – What are you seeking to understand, Fly? The derivative? Meaning? Or the meaning of the derivative? Or the derivative of meaning?

items.text: – Haha, Elder of the Tavern, Eldie, perfect. You hit the mark, Leopard Farid.

items.text: – Objectively, just because we arrived a few days late, these Tehran kids, who only got into AmirKabir thanks to localization, act like we're the ones who came in through a quota, not them. Objectively.
items.q: Sajad complains that Tehran students treat them as if they got in unfairly. Does this read naturally?

items.text: – Yeah. Don't let this Arasteh fool you; goofy as he is, his Konkoor rank was seventy-four.
items.q: Hooman brags about Amir's top rank in the national entrance exam. Does 'goofy as he is' sound natural?

items.text: – They killed Gaddafi. Objectively, come watch the video.
items.q: Sajad's habit word 'Objectively' pops up even here. Does it sound like a funny verbal tic?
